Side quest
SYDE kwest
noun (Gen-Z slang)
From role-playing games. Tabletop games such as Dungeons & Dragons (1974) and later video RPGs (The Legend of Zelda, The Elder Scrolls) divide a player’s tasks into the main quest, which advances the story, and optional side quests, which earn rewards along the way. Around 2021–2022 TikTok made side quest an everyday word for an unplanned detour: going out for milk and ending up helping a stranger move a couch.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

In current slang a side quest is a diversion from the main task — sometimes a pointless distraction ("I was supposed to study but I went on a side quest about medieval spoons"), sometimes a delightful detour that became the best part of the day. The Christian observation: Scripture names both kinds. There is the side quest that steals the main one. Martha was busy with many things, and Jesus gently told her, "But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part" (Luk 10:42). Paul would not be pulled off course: "this one thing I do" (Php 3:13), and "No man that warreth entangleth himself with the affairs of this life" (2Ti 2:4). "Let thine eyes look right on" (Pro 4:25). But there is also the side quest that was really the main quest in disguise. The priest and the Levite were too busy with their errands to stop; the Samaritan, "as he journeyed, came where he was: and when he saw him, he had compassion on him" (Luk 10:33). His detour is the story Jesus told to define what loving a neighbour means. A father teaches his son to tell the two apart: the phone, the rabbit hole, the hobby that eats the homework are side quests to refuse; the hurting person God puts on your road is not a side quest at all.

Webster 1828 Definition

Gen-Z slang (role-playing games; TikTok c. 2021–2022) for an unplanned diversion from the main task — Scripture warns against distractions that steal the one thing needful, and makes the Samaritan’s detour the main quest.

SIDE QUEST, n. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2021–present; gaming origin) A diversion or detour from one’s main task, planned or not. "Went to get gas and ended up on a side quest to return a lost dog."

To go on a side quest; side-questing. Often self-mocking about procrastination; sometimes proud of an adventure.

In role-playing games: an optional mission apart from the main quest, which carries the story.

Webster (1828), root word quest: “QUEST, noun [&hellip;] 1. The act of seeking; search; as, to rove in quest of game; to go in quest of a lost child; in quest of property, etc. 2. Inquest; a jury. [&hellip;] 3. Searchers, collectively. [&hellip;] 4. Inquiry; examination. [&hellip;] 5. Request; desire; solicitation.”

Decode for parents: ask whether it was a distraction or a neighbour. One should be refused; the other may be God’s appointment.

Key Scripture

Luk 10:42 — "But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her."

Php 3:13 — "Brethren, I count not myself to have apprehended: but this one thing I do, forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before,"

2Ti 2:4 — "No man that warreth entangleth himself with the affairs of this life; that he may please him who hath chosen him to be a soldier."

Pro 4:25 — "Let thine eyes look right on, and let thine eyelids look straight before thee."

Luk 10:33 — "But a certain Samaritan, as he journeyed, came where he was: and when he saw him, he had compassion on him,"

Modern Corruption

Side quest can dress up distraction as adventure; Scripture calls believers to the one thing needful, and also teaches that the neighbour in the ditch is never a detour.

expand to see more

A generation with a phone in its pocket lives on side quests. Every notification is an optional mission, and an hour of homework becomes four of clicking. Calling it a side quest makes the drift sound like an adventure, which is the oldest trick distraction has. Scripture’s answer is focus: Paul could say "this one thing I do" (Php 3:13), and he compared the Christian to a soldier who does not entangle himself with the affairs of this life (2Ti 2:4). Martha was not doing anything wicked; she was simply so busy with the side quests of hospitality that she missed the Guest (Luk 10:42).

Yet Jesus also told the story of a detour that was the whole point. The priest and the Levite stayed on task; the Samaritan stopped (Luk 10:33). The test is not whether the plan changed but whether love changed it. A rabbit hole that steals your duties is a side quest to refuse; the lonely kid at lunch, the widow who needs her gutters cleared, the stranger in the ditch are God’s appointments. Teach your children to let their eyes look right on (Pro 4:25) and to keep their hearts open to the ditch.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin quaerere (to seek) → English quest → tabletop and video RPGs: main quest vs. side quest → c. 2021–2022 TikTok: any detour from the plan.

expand to see more

Latin quaerere — to seek; Old French queste

Medieval romance: the knight’s quest, as for the Grail

1970s tabletop role-playing games; 1980s–2000s video RPGs

Side quest: an optional mission off the main storyline

c. 2021–2022 TikTok: real-life side quests

Usage

""Was supposed to finish my essay, went on a two-hour side quest about sharks.""

"One thing is needful (Luk 10:42); refuse the side quests that steal it."

"The Samaritan’s detour was the main quest (Luk 10:33)."
